items.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: most of their playing is done with their Jamey Aebersold play along records

ctx.x: You had an awful lot of good advice and guidance. Would you have anything to say to a young trumpet player who might not have the kind of foundation that you had but was still aspiring to a career in jazz? Nothing like ending with an easy question.

No, that’s a good one. It’s something I’ve put some thought into. I’ve had some students and occasionally have private students so it’s something I’ve thought about. I think for a young aspiring jazz trumpet player of course you’ve got to listen to some of the great records and do your homework as I said, you know, go back and listen to Louis Armstrong and listen to the greats throughout history. And put it together in your own way. And then also, I think one of the most important things that a lot of the young…

And they go out and play a gig and they might as well be playing along with the record. They’re not interacting, which is one of the big joys and important things in jazz that some people overlook or forget about, that it’s really supposed to be about this magical kind of interaction where you’re listening to him and you pick up a little thing that he did and he bounces off of you, and this guy is playing harmony, and you can’t really learn to do that otherwise than from just doing it. You just have to get out…
